content: Performance status in medicine, particularly in oncology and other related fields, is a clinical measure used to assess the overall well-being and functional capacity of cancer patients. This evaluation helps determine whether a patient is fit to undergo chemotherapy, whether adjustments to the treatment dose are necessary, and the level of palliative care required. Additionally, performance status is often utilized in oncological randomized controlled trials as an indicator of a patient’s quality of life. There are several scoring systems used to measure performance status. The most commonly employed are the Karnofsky Performance Scale and the ECOG/WHO/Zubrod scale, with the latter frequently appearing in publications by the World Health Organization (WHO). For pediatric patients, the Lansky Performance Scale is typically used. Other parallel scoring systems include the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) score, which is integrated as the fifth axis in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM) of psychiatry. The Karnofsky Performance Scale ranges from 100 to 0, where a score of 100 represents perfect health, and 0 indicates death. Although the scale is traditionally described in intervals of 10, clinicians may use decimal points to reflect a patient’s condition more precisely if it falls between two defined levels. This scale was developed by Dr. David A. Karnofsky and Dr. Joseph H. Burchenal in 1949. The specific levels of the Karnofsky scale are as follows: 100%: The patient is in normal health, with no complaints or signs of disease. 90%: The patient is capable of normal activity, with only minor symptoms or signs of disease. 80%: The patient can perform normal activities but experiences some difficulty and has noticeable symptoms or signs. 70%: The patient can care for themselves but is unable to carry out normal activities or work. 60%: The patient requires some assistance but can manage most personal needs independently. 50%: The patient frequently requires help and needs regular medical care. 40%: The patient is disabled and requires special care and assistance. 30%: The patient is severely disabled, with hospital admission indicated, but there is no immediate risk of death. 20%: The patient is critically ill, urgently requiring hospital admission and supportive treatments. 10%: The patient is moribund, with rapidly progressing fatal disease processes. 0%: The patient is deceased. The ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) score, also known as the WHO or Zubrod score, was published by Oken et al. in 1982. This scoring system is another widely used method for assessing performance status in clinical and research settings.
